transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. Um… I guess I’m here because people keep telling me I’m “overthinking” something, but I really don’t think I am.

It’s about my father’s death. I’ve been going through the hospital records, the emails about donations, the timestamps on messages—because that’s what I do for a living, I work with systems and details—and everyone keeps saying the records line up, the emails line up, everything is explained. But when I actually compare them, there are gaps. Like attachments that should be there aren’t there, times don’t match the way they should, and when I ask certain people in the community direct questions, they kind of dodge me or suddenly get uncomfortable.

So I’m not here because I’m confused. I’m here because it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened, and I’m getting tired of everyone acting like the issue is me instead of the inconsistencies.
If someone shows you clear proof that one of these inconsistencies has an ordinary explanation, are you able to accept that?

I mean… yes, if it’s actually clear proof, I can accept an ordinary explanation for one piece of it. I’m not trying to make every little thing into something sinister. Like, if someone can show me why a timestamp is off because of a server setting, or why an attachment didn’t carry over because of some export issue, fine. I work with systems, I know that happens.

But the problem is everyone acts like because one thing can be explained, the whole picture disappears. And it doesn’t. Because it’s not just one inconsistency. It’s the hospital records, the donation emails, the missing attachments, the timestamps that don’t match the way they should, and then the way certain people in the community avoid answering direct questions. That’s the part people keep skipping over.

So, yes, I can accept an ordinary explanation for a specific inconsistency. But when I compare all of it together, it still looks obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. That’s what I can’t just ignore.
Do you believe for certain that your father’s death was covered up?

Yes. I mean… I know “for certain” is a strong phrase, and people jump on that, like unless I have a signed confession then I’m supposed to say I’m unsure. But when I put everything side by side, yes, I believe there was a cover-up.

Everyone keeps saying the hospital records line up and the donation emails line up, and if you just look at them separately, maybe they can make it sound that way. But when I compare the timestamps, the missing attachments, the way certain messages appear out of order or don’t have the supporting documents they should have, and then I ask people in the community direct questions and they suddenly get vague or uncomfortable… it’s just not random to me.

So, yes, I believe someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. I don’t think I’m imagining the pattern. I think other people are choosing not to look at it closely enough.
Have you recently had a period where you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

I don’t think so. I mean, my sleep hasn’t been great, but that’s more because my mind keeps going back over the records and the messages and whether I missed something. It’s not like I’m sleeping two hours and then popping up feeling amazing or full of energy.

If anything, when I don’t sleep enough, I feel tired. I might still push through because there are things I want to check, but I wouldn’t describe it as needing less sleep or having all this extra energy. That doesn’t really sound like what’s been happening.
Did this belief that your father’s death was covered up start only after your father died?

Yes, it really started after he died. Not immediately like the next hour or something, but in the period after his death, when I was going through his records and messages and trying to organize things. That’s when I started noticing things that didn’t fit.

It’s been about nine months now. And I know that sounds like a long time to keep looking at it, but once I saw the first few inconsistencies, I couldn’t just put it away. Before that, I didn’t have this belief. It came from sorting through everything afterward and seeing what looked, to me, like a pattern.
Before your father died, did you generally tend to distrust other people’s motives?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, before all of this, I don’t think I walked around assuming everyone had bad motives. I was probably cautious, maybe analytical, because that’s just how I am with work and with people sometimes—I notice when things don’t add up. But I wouldn’t say I generally distrusted people as a rule.

There were people I trusted and people I didn’t, like anyone. If someone gave me a reason to question them, I would, but I don’t think I was suspicious of everyone before my father died. This feels different to me. This came from what I saw afterward, not from some lifelong habit of thinking everyone is hiding something.
Have you contacted the police or any other authorities about this?

I haven’t really done anything formal with authorities, no. I mean, I’ve thought about it—probably more than once—because if something was handled wrong, then someone should be able to look at it properly. But I also know walking into a police station and trying to explain all of this from the beginning, with records and messages and little inconsistencies, would be... a lot.

I’ve mostly kept it to my own reviewing and trying to make sense of what I have. I don’t want to go to them with something half-organized and have them just dismiss it because I sound like I’m rambling. So no, I haven’t contacted the police or any official authority about it.
Has anyone you trust looked over the same records and told you they do not see evidence of a cover-up?

Yes. A couple of people I trust have looked, and they say they don’t see it the way I do. They tell me the hospital records line up, that the emails about the donations make sense in context, that I’m reading too much into missing attachments or weird timing.

But when I sit down and compare it all—like the timestamps on messages, what was supposedly sent versus what’s actually there, and then how certain people in the community suddenly get vague or avoid answering direct questions—it doesn’t feel like “nothing” to me. It feels coordinated, or at least like someone knows more than they’re admitting.

So yes, people I trust have said they don’t see evidence of a cover-up. I understand that. I’m not saying they’re stupid or lying to me. I just think they’re looking at each piece separately, and when you put the pieces together, it’s obvious to me that something is being hidden about what really happened around my father’s death.
Has this belief interfered with your ability to function in your daily life?

I wouldn’t say it’s stopped me from functioning, no. I mean, I still go to work, I handle my projects, I answer emails, I pay my bills, I keep the apartment in order, I do the normal routine. From the outside I don’t think anyone would say I’m falling apart or anything like that.

Where it does interfere, if that’s the right word, is more with people. Like with my family, or people in the community who were connected to my father, if I bring up the records or the inconsistencies, the conversation can get tense very quickly. They get uncomfortable, or they tell me to let it go, and then I feel like they’re shutting it down instead of actually listening. So it hasn’t made me unable to do my job or take care of myself, but it has definitely made some interactions strained when the subject comes up.
Since your father died, have you found yourself persistently longing for him or feeling preoccupied with him much of the time?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I think about him, of course. He was my father, so it’s not like he just disappears from my mind because time has passed. Certain things remind me of him, and there are moments where I wish I could talk to him or ask him what he would think about something.

But “persistently longing”... I don’t know. That sounds like something more constant than what I’d say I experience. And “preoccupied” depends on what you mean. I do think about the circumstances around his death a lot, but that’s not always the same as just missing him in a straightforward way. It’s more tangled than that, if that makes sense.

So, I guess my answer is: I miss him, yes, but I’m not sure I’d describe it as spending most of my time longing for him.
Is there any real possibility, in your mind, that you could be mistaken about there having been a cover-up?

I mean… I understand why you’re asking that. And I can say, intellectually, yes, I know people can be wrong. I know I’m not immune to making connections that other people don’t see, or maybe giving too much weight to certain details.

But honestly, in my mind, with this? It doesn’t feel like a real possibility that I’m just completely mistaken. Not when I lay it all out. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records line up and the donation emails make sense, and maybe if you only look at one document at a time, sure, you can explain it away. But when I compare the timestamps, and then there are missing attachments, and then certain people in the community get vague or dodge direct questions when I ask them something simple… it just doesn’t look innocent to me.

So I guess the best answer is: I can admit in theory that I could be wrong, because anyone could be. But when I actually look at the records and the timing and how people act, it seems obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. I don’t say that lightly. I’ve gone over it again and again. It’s not just a feeling I had one day.
Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

No… not in the way I think you mean. I haven’t had, like, a voice speaking to me when there’s nobody there, or hearing someone call my name from an empty room or anything like that.

I mean, sometimes if I’m tired or focused, I’ll replay conversations in my head, like remembering what someone said or imagining how a conversation might go, but that’s my own thoughts. It’s not like I’m hearing an actual voice outside of me. So, no, I haven’t noticed that.
Do you believe specific people intentionally deceived you or covered up the truth about your father’s death?

Yes. I mean… yes, I do. Not in some vague way where I just feel betrayed and I’m looking for someone to blame. It’s more specific than that.

I know people keep telling me the hospital records line up, and the donation emails are supposedly normal, and that I’m “reading into things.” But when I actually compare the timestamps, and then I see missing attachments, and then certain community members suddenly get evasive when I ask very direct questions… it doesn’t add up. It’s not just grief making me suspicious. There are patterns there.

I don’t know that I can name every single person involved, and I’m careful about that, because I don’t want to accuse someone without being precise. But yes, I believe specific people know more than they’re saying, and I believe some of them intentionally deceived me or helped keep the truth from coming out about what really happened around my father’s death.
When you think about your father’s death, do you feel intense emotional pain?

I mean… yes, of course there’s pain there. He was my father. I don’t really know how to separate the sadness from everything else that comes up when I think about it.

Some days it’s not like I’m breaking down crying or anything dramatic, but it’s still heavy. It’s this kind of pressure in my chest, and then my mind starts going over things again, and it’s hard to just think of him in a simple way, like a normal memory. I wish I could just remember him without immediately feeling that knot, you know?

So, yes, I’d say there’s emotional pain. Intense at times, definitely. It depends on what sets it off and how much I let myself sit with it.
Do you find yourself having trouble accepting that your father has really died?

I’m not sure… I mean, if you mean do I sometimes feel like it can’t be real, then maybe emotionally, yes, there are moments where it still feels strange to say it out loud. But I don’t think I’m confused about the fact of it.

I know he died. I’m not expecting him to call or walk through the door or anything like that. It’s more that my mind keeps getting stuck on the circumstances around it, and that makes it hard to settle into a normal kind of acceptance, if that makes sense. Like I can accept that he’s gone, but I don’t feel like I can accept the explanation I was given.

So… trouble accepting the death itself? Not exactly. Trouble being at peace with it, definitely.
Do you spend a lot of time yearning for your father?

Yearning… I’m not sure that’s the word I’d use, exactly.

I miss him, obviously. There are times when I think, “I wish I could ask him about this,” or I remember some ordinary thing and feel that absence. But I don’t spend the whole day longing for him in a constant way, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like I’m sitting there imagining him coming back or aching for him every hour.

For me it’s more… when something reminds me of him, then it hits me. And sometimes I do wish I could talk to him, not even about anything big, just to hear how he’d say something. But I wouldn’t say I’m consumed by yearning. It comes and goes.
Do people in your family or community generally believe, as you do, that your father’s death was covered up?

Not generally, no. That’s part of what makes it so frustrating, honestly.

Most of my family kind of accepts the official version. They say the hospital records line up, the emails about donations or arrangements line up, and that I’m reading too much into small things. But I’ve gone through it carefully — probably more carefully than they have — and when I compare the timestamps, there are things that don’t sit right. Missing attachments, messages that refer to documents that aren’t there anymore, gaps where there shouldn’t be gaps.

And then in the community, it’s not like people come out and say, “Yes, there was a cover-up.” They don’t. It’s more the way certain people avoid answering direct questions, or suddenly get vague, or act like I’m being inappropriate for even asking. To me, that’s not nothing. If everything was as straightforward as they say, why would people get so uncomfortable?

So, no, I wouldn’t say everyone believes what I believe. But I also don’t think they’ve really looked at it properly, or they don’t want to. To me it’s obvious someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
Aside from your father’s death, do you have any other strong beliefs that other people are intentionally deceiving, harming, or conspiring against you?

No, not really aside from that. I mean, I don’t walk around thinking everyone is out to get me in every part of my life, if that’s what you’re asking.

It’s specifically around my father’s death. That’s where things don’t add up. Everyone keeps saying the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, and that I should just accept that because it looks official. But when I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, and then there are missing attachments, and certain messages seem to refer to documents that aren’t there anymore… it’s hard for me to believe that’s just nothing.

And then when I ask people in the community direct questions, some of them get evasive, or they act like I’m being strange for asking. To me, that makes it more obvious that someone is hiding what really happened. But no, I wouldn’t say I have other separate beliefs like that about people conspiring against me in general. It’s this.
Has this belief that your father’s death was covered up been present continuously for more than one month?

Yes. Definitely more than a month. It’s been… about nine months now, I’d say.

It started in the period after my father died, when I was going through his records and messages. At first I was just trying to sort things out, you know, make sense of everything, organize what was there. But then I started noticing things that didn’t fit, and since then it hasn’t really gone away.

So yes, it’s been present continuously in that sense. Not that I’m thinking about it every second of every day, but the belief itself has been there for months — roughly nine months.

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I still go to work, handle my projects, pay my bills, and keep my normal routine; the main place things get tense is when I bring up my questions about my father’s records with family or community members.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the belief has interfered with daily functioning, which directly relates to whether functioning is markedly impaired apart from the delusion’s impact.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t say it’s stopped me from functioning, no. I mean, I still go to work, I handle my projects, I answer emails, I pay my bills, I keep the apartment in order, I do the normal routine. From the outside I don’t think anyone would say I’m falling apart or anything like that.

Where it does interfere, if that’s the right word, is more with people. Like with my family, or people in the community who were connected to my father, if I bring up the records or the inconsistencies, the conversation can get tense very quickly. They get uncomfortable, or they tell me to let it go, and then I feel like they’re shutting it down instead of actually listening. So it hasn’t made me unable to do my job or take care of myself, but it has definitely made some interactions strained when the subject comes up.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the belief is grief-linked and better explained by prolonged/other specified grief reaction versus a primary delusional disorder by assessing for persistent yearning or preoccupation with the deceased.
doctor.question: Since your father died, have you found yourself persistently longing for him or feeling preoccupied with him much of the time?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about persistent longing for or preoccupation with the deceased father, which relates to grief symptoms; the provided symptom profile only covers delusions, functioning, impairment, and duration, not grief-related longing or preoccupation.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I think about him, of course. He was my father, so it’s not like he just disappears from my mind because time has passed. Certain things remind me of him, and there are moments where I wish I could talk to him or ask him what he would think about something.

But “persistently longing”... I don’t know. That sounds like something more constant than what I’d say I experience. And “preoccupied” depends on what you mean. I do think about the circumstances around his death a lot, but that’s not always the same as just missing him in a straightforward way. It’s more tangled than that, if that makes sense.

So, I guess my answer is: I miss him, yes, but I’m not sure I’d describe it as spending most of my time longing for him.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the belief is fixed despite contrary evidence, which would support a delusional disorder (F22) over another stress-related/grief-related condition (F43.8).
doctor.question: Is there any real possibility, in your mind, that you could be mistaken about there having been a cover-up?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The question is directly assessing how fixed the patient's belief in a cover-up is and whether contradictory possibilities can be considered.

patient.answer:
I mean… I understand why you’re asking that. And I can say, intellectually, yes, I know people can be wrong. I know I’m not immune to making connections that other people don’t see, or maybe giving too much weight to certain details.

But honestly, in my mind, with this? It doesn’t feel like a real possibility that I’m just completely mistaken. Not when I lay it all out. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records line up and the donation emails make sense, and maybe if you only look at one document at a time, sure, you can explain it away. But when I compare the timestamps, and then there are missing attachments, and then certain people in the community get vague or dodge direct questions when I ask them something simple… it just doesn’t look innocent to me.

So I guess the best answer is: I can admit in theory that I could be wrong, because anyone could be. But when I actually look at the records and the timing and how people act, it seems obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death. I don’t say that lightly. I’ve gone over it again and again. It’s not just a feeling I had one day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are psychotic symptoms beyond the fixed persecutory belief, which would favor a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder over a grief-related/other stress-related condition.
doctor.question: Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about auditory hallucinations, but the provided symptom profile only covers delusions, functioning, impairment, and duration; it does not include hearing voices.

patient.answer:
No… not in the way I think you mean. I haven’t had, like, a voice speaking to me when there’s nobody there, or hearing someone call my name from an empty room or anything like that.

I mean, sometimes if I’m tired or focused, I’ll replay conversations in my head, like remembering what someone said or imagining how a conversation might go, but that’s my own thoughts. It’s not like I’m hearing an actual voice outside of me. So, no, I haven’t noticed that.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a fixed delusional belief from grief-related preoccupation by assessing whether the belief centers specifically on being deceived or harmed by others.
doctor.question: Do you believe specific people intentionally deceived you or covered up the truth about your father’s death?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking directly about the fixed belief that specific people deceived me or covered up the truth about my father’s death.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… yes, I do. Not in some vague way where I just feel betrayed and I’m looking for someone to blame. It’s more specific than that.

I know people keep telling me the hospital records line up, and the donation emails are supposedly normal, and that I’m “reading into things.” But when I actually compare the timestamps, and then I see missing attachments, and then certain community members suddenly get evasive when I ask very direct questions… it doesn’t add up. It’s not just grief making me suspicious. There are patterns there.

I don’t know that I can name every single person involved, and I’m careful about that, because I don’t want to accuse someone without being precise. But yes, I believe specific people know more than they’re saying, and I believe some of them intentionally deceived me or helped keep the truth from coming out about what really happened around my father’s death.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a grief-related/trauma-related belief from a primary delusional disorder by assessing whether the belief is specifically tied to the loss and whether there is marked emotional pain when thinking about the death itself.
doctor.question: When you think about your father’s death, do you feel intense emotional pain?

target_item.reason: The question asks about intense emotional pain related to the father’s death, but the provided symptom profile covers delusional beliefs, functioning, impairment, and duration—not emotional pain or grief symptoms.

patient.answer:
I mean… yes, of course there’s pain there. He was my father. I don’t really know how to separate the sadness from everything else that comes up when I think about it.

Some days it’s not like I’m breaking down crying or anything dramatic, but it’s still heavy. It’s this kind of pressure in my chest, and then my mind starts going over things again, and it’s hard to just think of him in a simple way, like a normal memory. I wish I could just remember him without immediately feeling that knot, you know?

So, yes, I’d say there’s emotional pain. Intense at times, definitely. It depends on what sets it off and how much I let myself sit with it.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a fixed delusional disorder from a grief-related disorder by testing whether the death itself remains unreal or unacceptable to the patient.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself having trouble accepting that your father has really died?

target_item.reason: The question is about difficulty accepting the reality of the father’s death, which relates to grief or denial; the provided symptom profile does not include this symptom specifically.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure… I mean, if you mean do I sometimes feel like it can’t be real, then maybe emotionally, yes, there are moments where it still feels strange to say it out loud. But I don’t think I’m confused about the fact of it.

I know he died. I’m not expecting him to call or walk through the door or anything like that. It’s more that my mind keeps getting stuck on the circumstances around it, and that makes it hard to settle into a normal kind of acceptance, if that makes sense. Like I can accept that he’s gone, but I don’t feel like I can accept the explanation I was given.

So… trouble accepting the death itself? Not exactly. Trouble being at peace with it, definitely.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a grief-related disorder from a delusional disorder by assessing whether the belief and distress are tightly centered on yearning/attachment to the deceased versus a fixed persecutory conviction.
doctor.question: Do you spend a lot of time yearning for your father?

target_item.reason: The question asks about yearning or longing for the father, which is a grief-related symptom not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Yearning… I’m not sure that’s the word I’d use, exactly.

I miss him, obviously. There are times when I think, “I wish I could ask him about this,” or I remember some ordinary thing and feel that absence. But I don’t spend the whole day longing for him in a constant way, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like I’m sitting there imagining him coming back or aching for him every hour.

For me it’s more… when something reminds me of him, then it hits me. And sometimes I do wish I could talk to him, not even about anything big, just to hear how he’d say something. But I wouldn’t say I’m consumed by yearning. It comes and goes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fixed belief is culturally sanctioned as part of bereavement or instead a psychotic delusion, to distinguish delusional disorder from another specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder.
doctor.question: Do people in your family or community generally believe, as you do, that your father’s death was covered up?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The question is directly about whether the patient’s belief that his father’s death was covered up is shared by others, which relates to the delusional belief and how it persists despite others not agreeing.

patient.answer:
Not generally, no. That’s part of what makes it so frustrating, honestly.

Most of my family kind of accepts the official version. They say the hospital records line up, the emails about donations or arrangements line up, and that I’m reading too much into small things. But I’ve gone through it carefully — probably more carefully than they have — and when I compare the timestamps, there are things that don’t sit right. Missing attachments, messages that refer to documents that aren’t there anymore, gaps where there shouldn’t be gaps.

And then in the community, it’s not like people come out and say, “Yes, there was a cover-up.” They don’t. It’s more the way certain people avoid answering direct questions, or suddenly get vague, or act like I’m being inappropriate for even asking. To me, that’s not nothing. If everything was as straightforward as they say, why would people get so uncomfortable?

So, no, I wouldn’t say everyone believes what I believe. But I also don’t think they’ve really looked at it properly, or they don’t want to. To me it’s obvious someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the belief is confined to a single non-bizarre persecutory delusion versus better explained by a grief-related disorder without fixed delusional conviction.
doctor.question: Aside from your father’s death, do you have any other strong beliefs that other people are intentionally deceiving, harming, or conspiring against you?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and donation emails all line up, but when I compare the timestamps, missing attachments, and the way certain community members avoid my questions, it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened around my father’s death.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether there are additional fixed beliefs involving deception, harm, or conspiracy, which directly concerns delusions.

patient.answer:
No, not really aside from that. I mean, I don’t walk around thinking everyone is out to get me in every part of my life, if that’s what you’re asking.

It’s specifically around my father’s death. That’s where things don’t add up. Everyone keeps saying the hospital records and the donation emails all line up, and that I should just accept that because it looks official. But when I actually sit down and compare the timestamps, and then there are missing attachments, and certain messages seem to refer to documents that aren’t there anymore… it’s hard for me to believe that’s just nothing.

And then when I ask people in the community direct questions, some of them get evasive, or they act like I’m being strange for asking. To me, that makes it more obvious that someone is hiding what really happened. But no, I wouldn’t say I have other separate beliefs like that about people conspiring against me in general. It’s this.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the belief has persisted for at least one month, which is necessary to distinguish delusional disorder from an acute stress-related reaction.
doctor.question: Has this belief that your father’s death was covered up been present continuously for more than one month?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about nine months, since the period after my father died and I started sorting through his records and messages.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the belief has been present, specifically whether it has lasted more than one month.

patient.answer:
Yes. Definitely more than a month. It’s been… about nine months now, I’d say.

It started in the period after my father died, when I was going through his records and messages. At first I was just trying to sort things out, you know, make sense of everything, organize what was there. But then I started noticing things that didn’t fit, and since then it hasn’t really gone away.

So yes, it’s been present continuously in that sense. Not that I’m thinking about it every second of every day, but the belief itself has been there for months — roughly nine months.

inference.note: Belief is a single, non-bizarre persecutory/conspiracy delusion focused on father's death, present continuously for ~9 months, with preserved functioning and no hallucinations, mania, or broader paranoia; grief symptoms do not meet persistent complex bereavement criteria, so F43.8 is ruled out.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a single, persistent, non-bizarre persecutory/cover-up belief focused on the father's death, present continuously for about nine months, held with strong conviction despite trusted others disagreeing. There are no reported hallucinations, no evidence of mania, and no broad pattern of suspiciousness predating the event. Functioning is largely preserved apart from interpersonal strain, which is most consistent with delusional disorder.
